title: API Gateways & Ingress Controllers
summary: A Service exposes pods inside the cluster — but how do external HTTP requests reach the right service? Ingress is the Kubernetes resource that defines routing rules; Ingress Controllers (nginx, Traefik, Envoy) are the actual reverse proxies that implement them. The newer Gateway API addresses Ingress limitations with a richer, role-oriented model. This lesson covers both, plus real-world patterns: TLS termination, path routing, rate limiting, and authentication.

sections.title: Ingress: exposing HTTP services externally
sections.body:
## How External Traffic Reaches Kubernetes Services

A Kubernetes `Service` of type `ClusterIP` is only reachable from inside the cluster. To expose an application to external users, you have three options built into Kubernetes: `NodePort` (binds a port on every node — awkward in production), `LoadBalancer` (provisions a cloud load balancer per service — expensive), or `Ingress` (one entry point, routing rules in-cluster).

**Ingress** is the standard answer for HTTP/HTTPS workloads. It separates two concerns: the **routing rules** (which URLs go to which service) are defined in `Ingress` resources managed by application teams, while the **reverse proxy** that implements those rules (the Ingress Controller) is managed by the platform team and runs as a deployment inside the cluster. This separation means application teams can update routing without touching infrastructure, and the platform team can upgrade or replace the controller without touching application manifests.

The Ingress Controller watches the Kubernetes API for `Ingress` objects and continuously reconciles its internal configuration to match. For nginx-based controllers, this means regenerating an `nginx.conf` and triggering a graceful reload. For Envoy-based controllers (like Contour or the Emissary Ingress), it means updating xDS configuration dynamically without any reloads.

**TLS termination** at the Ingress layer is the canonical pattern: the controller handles the TLS handshake with external clients, and traffic between the controller and your backend services travels over plain HTTP inside the cluster (or over mTLS if you have a service mesh). This keeps TLS certificate management centralized — your application code does not need to be aware of certificates at all.

Understanding `IngressClass` is important in clusters with multiple controllers. A cluster might run both nginx (for general HTTP routing) and an AWS ALB controller (for workloads needing AWS-native features). `IngressClass` specifies which controller handles a given `Ingress` resource, preventing conflicts.

**The problem Ingress solves:**

```
Without Ingress — one LoadBalancer per service:
  Service A → LoadBalancer (IP: 1.2.3.4:80)
  Service B → LoadBalancer (IP: 1.2.3.5:80)
  Service C → LoadBalancer (IP: 1.2.3.6:80)
  → Expensive: each cloud LB costs ~$20/month
  → No shared TLS, no path routing

With Ingress — one entry point, rules-based routing:
  nginx Ingress Controller → LoadBalancer (IP: 1.2.3.4:443)
    /api/*   → backend-service:8000
    /app/*   → frontend-service:80
    /static/ → cdn-service:80
  → One LB, shared TLS cert, path-based routing
```

**Ingress resource — defines routing rules:**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    # Controller-specific annotations go here
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx         # Which controller handles this Ingress
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - app.example.com
    secretName: app-tls            # TLS cert stored as a Secret
  rules:
  - host: app.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix            # Prefix | Exact | ImplementationSpecific
        backend:
          service:
            name: backend-service
            port:
              number: 8000
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: frontend-service
            port:
              number: 80
```

**IngressClass — which controller handles this Ingress:**

```bash
# List available ingress classes in the cluster
kubectl get ingressclass
# NAME    CONTROLLER             PARAMETERS   AGE
# nginx   k8s.io/ingress-nginx   <none>       2d

# Set a default IngressClass (no need to specify ingressClassName on every Ingress)
kubectl annotate ingressclass nginx \
  ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true
```

**pathType matters:**

```
Exact:    /foo    matches /foo only (not /foo/bar)
Prefix:   /foo    matches /foo, /foo/, /foo/bar, /foo/bar/baz
ImplementationSpecific: regex or other controller-defined matching

# nginx-specific: regex matching with ~ prefix
annotations:
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/use-regex: "true"
# Then path: /api/v[0-9]+/.*
```

sections.title: nginx Ingress Controller: TLS, redirects, and annotations
sections.body:
## The nginx Ingress Controller in Depth

The nginx Ingress Controller is the most widely deployed Kubernetes ingress solution, running in the majority of on-premises and self-managed Kubernetes clusters. Its model is straightforward: it runs nginx as a reverse proxy, watches the Kubernetes API for `Ingress` resources, and translates those resources into nginx `server` and `location` blocks. When you create or update an `Ingress`, the controller generates a new `nginx.conf` and performs a graceful reload.

The controller's behavior is extended primarily through **annotations** — key-value metadata on the `Ingress` resource that the controller interprets as configuration directives. This design predates the Gateway API and is why annotations feel like a parallel configuration language bolted onto Kubernetes. Annotations are controller-specific: `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps` only works with the nginx controller; the same behavior in Traefik uses a different annotation with different semantics. This lack of standardization across controllers is one of the primary motivations for the Gateway API.

**TLS termination** is a critical security boundary. When the controller terminates TLS, it needs access to the certificate and private key, which are stored as a Kubernetes `Secret` of type `kubernetes.io/tls`. In production, you never manage these manually — `cert-manager` handles issuance and rotation automatically, integrating with Let's Encrypt (for public domains) or an internal CA (for private infrastructure). The controller watches for Secret updates and reloads its TLS configuration without downtime.

**Rate limiting at the ingress layer** is a defense-in-depth measure. It protects your backends from traffic spikes and brute-force attacks before the request ever reaches your application code. The nginx controller implements rate limiting using nginx's `limit_req` module, which uses a leaky bucket algorithm. Understanding the `limit-rps` (sustained rate) and `limit-burst-multiplier` (burst headroom) settings is important — setting the burst too low causes false positives on legitimate traffic spikes; setting it too high defeats the purpose of rate limiting.

**Nginx Ingress Controller is the most widely deployed — it translates Ingress objects into nginx config:**

```bash
# Install nginx ingress controller (in this lab k3s has Traefik disabled,
# so we can install nginx)
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx --create-namespace \
  --set controller.service.type=NodePort  # No cloud LB in local cluster
```

**TLS termination — the controller handles HTTPS, upstream gets HTTP:**

```bash
# Create a self-signed cert for local testing
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 \
  -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -subj "/CN=app.local/O=DevOps Lab"

# Store as a TLS Secret
kubectl create secret tls app-tls \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key \
  -n production
```

**cert-manager — automatic TLS from Let's Encrypt:**

```yaml
# With cert-manager installed, Ingress gets auto-renewed certs
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod  # triggers cert provisioning
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts: [app.example.com]
    secretName: app-tls   # cert-manager creates and updates this Secret
```

**Common nginx ingress annotations:**

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    # Force HTTPS redirect
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"

    # Rate limiting — 100 requests per minute per IP
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "100"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "20"

    # Timeouts
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-connect-timeout: "10"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "60"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "60"

    # Body size limit (default 1m — increase for file uploads)
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "50m"

    # CORS
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/enable-cors: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/cors-allow-origin: "https://app.example.com"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/cors-allow-methods: "GET, POST, OPTIONS"

    # Basic auth
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-type: basic
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-secret: basic-auth-secret
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-realm: "Protected Area"

    # OAuth2 proxy (external auth)
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url: "http://oauth2-proxy/oauth2/auth"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-signin: "http://oauth2-proxy/oauth2/sign_in"

    # Custom nginx config snippet
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet: |
      add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
      add_header X-Frame-Options DENY;
```

**Canary deployments with nginx Ingress:**

```yaml
# Route 10% of traffic to canary
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: my-app-canary
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"  # 10% to canary
spec:
  rules:
  - host: app.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: backend-canary
            port:
              number: 8000
```

sections.title: Gateway API: the next generation
sections.body:
## Gateway API: A Principled Replacement for Ingress

The Kubernetes Ingress API has served the community well for years, but it was designed with a narrow scope — HTTP routing with a single TLS endpoint — and the ecosystem has been papering over its limitations with controller-specific annotations ever since. The **Gateway API** is the SIG-Network project's answer: a richer, more expressive, and deliberately role-oriented set of resources that will eventually replace Ingress as the standard way to expose services.

The foundational insight behind Gateway API is that routing configuration is owned by **multiple distinct roles** with different concerns and different levels of trust:

- **Infrastructure owners** decide what type of load balancer or gateway hardware/software is used (GatewayClass).
- **Platform engineers** decide what ports, protocols, and TLS configurations are exposed (Gateway).
- **Application developers** decide what paths and hostnames route to their services (HTTPRoute, TCPRoute, GRPCRoute).

With the old `Ingress` resource, all of this is collapsed into one resource. An application developer who needs to change a path prefix must edit the same object that controls TLS configuration. In large organizations, this creates permission and change-management problems.

Gateway API also **standardizes features that were annotation-only** in Ingress. Traffic splitting (canary deployments), retry policies, request/response header manipulation, and request mirroring are first-class concepts in HTTPRoute — defined in spec fields with consistent schemas across all Gateway API implementations, not in free-form annotation strings that differ by controller.

Gateway API is already GA for core resources (`GatewayClass`, `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`) and is being adopted by every major controller: nginx, Traefik, Envoy Gateway, Istio, Linkerd, and cloud-native implementations from AWS, GCP, and Azure. Learning it now positions you for how routing will be configured across the entire Kubernetes ecosystem going forward.

**Why Gateway API replaces Ingress:**

Ingress has limitations that cause vendors to use non-standard annotations:
- No support for TCP/UDP routing (only HTTP)
- No role separation (same resource configures both infra and app routing)
- Every controller has different annotation naming
- No built-in support for traffic splitting, retries, or request mirroring

**Gateway API role model:**

```
GatewayClass  → Infrastructure team: which controller and what infrastructure
Gateway       → Platform team:      which ports/protocols/TLS to expose
HTTPRoute     → App team:           which paths route to which services
TCPRoute      → App team:           TCP routing rules
GRPCRoute     → App team:           gRPC routing rules
```

**GatewayClass — defines the type of Gateway (set by infra team):**

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  controllerName: k8s.nginx.org/nginx-gateway-controller
```

**Gateway — defines listeners (set by platform team):**

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: production-gateway
  namespace: infra
spec:
  gatewayClassName: nginx
  listeners:
  - name: https
    port: 443
    protocol: HTTPS
    tls:
      mode: Terminate
      certificateRefs:
      - name: wildcard-tls
        namespace: infra
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: All   # Routes from any namespace can attach
```

**HTTPRoute — defines routing rules (set by app team):**

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: checkout-route
  namespace: production
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: production-gateway
    namespace: infra          # Attach to the shared Gateway
  hostnames: ["checkout.example.com"]
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /api
    backendRefs:
    - name: checkout-api
      port: 8000
      weight: 90             # 90% to stable
    - name: checkout-api-canary
      port: 8000
      weight: 10             # 10% to canary
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /
    filters:
    - type: RequestHeaderModifier
      requestHeaderModifier:
        add:
        - name: X-Forwarded-Host
          value: checkout.example.com
    backendRefs:
    - name: checkout-frontend
      port: 80
```

**Gateway API vs Ingress:**

```
Feature                   Ingress     Gateway API
HTTP routing              ✓           ✓
TCP/UDP routing           ✗           ✓
Traffic splitting         annotation  native
Retry policies            annotation  native
Request mirroring         annotation  native
Role separation           ✗           ✓
Cross-namespace routing   ✗           ✓
Standardisation           ✗           ✓ (SIG-Network)
```

sections.title: Rate limiting and authentication patterns
sections.body:
## Rate Limiting and Authentication at the Gateway Layer

Security controls applied at the gateway layer are more efficient than the same controls applied inside individual application services. A request that is rate-limited or rejected at the ingress controller never touches your application servers, your databases, or your internal network — which matters both for performance under attack and for keeping application code simple.

**Rate limiting** protects against two threat classes: unintentional overload (a client bug sending thousands of requests) and intentional abuse (scraping, brute force, credential stuffing). Configuring it at the ingress layer gives you a single control point across all services. The key parameters to understand are the **rate** (sustained requests per second per key), the **burst** (headroom above the rate for short spikes), and the **key** (what uniquely identifies a client — by default the source IP, but you can key on API token headers for authenticated clients).

**Authentication patterns** at the gateway vary by threat model:

| Pattern | Use Case | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Basic auth** | Internal tools, admin dashboards | Simple but credentials travel with every request; requires HTTPS |
| **OAuth2 Proxy / OIDC** | User-facing apps integrated with SSO | Full OAuth flow; works with GitHub, Google, Okta, etc. |
| **JWT validation** | API-to-API, mobile clients | Stateless; no session storage needed; tokens can be short-lived |
| **mTLS** | Service-to-service, B2B APIs | Strongest: client identity is cryptographic, not credential-based |

**Kong Ingress Controller** is worth understanding separately because it blurs the line between Ingress controller and API gateway. Traditional ingress controllers (nginx, Traefik) focus on routing. Kong adds a plugin system — rate limiting, JWT validation, OAuth, request transformation, response caching — configured through Kubernetes CRDs. This is the "API gateway" capability layer that sits between a simple reverse proxy and a full-featured API management platform.

For most internal services, nginx annotations are sufficient. For public APIs with complex authentication, rate limiting by API key, and developer portal needs, a purpose-built API gateway like Kong, AWS API Gateway, or Apigee provides better operator experience and more granular controls.

**Rate limiting at the ingress layer — protect before requests reach your app:**

```yaml
# nginx Ingress — IP-based rate limiting
annotations:
  # 10 requests per second per IP (burst of 20 allowed)
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "10"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-burst-multiplier: "2"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "5"

  # Rate limit by a custom key (e.g., API key header)
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-req-zone-key: "$http_x_api_key"
```

**Kong Ingress Controller — full API gateway features:**

Kong is an API gateway built on nginx. The Kong Ingress Controller lets you configure Kong plugins via Kubernetes resources:

```yaml
# KongPlugin — define a reusable plugin config
apiVersion: configuration.konghq.com/v1
kind: KongPlugin
metadata:
  name: rate-limit-api
config:
  minute: 100
  hour: 10000
  policy: local
plugin: rate-limiting
---
# KongPlugin — JWT authentication
apiVersion: configuration.konghq.com/v1
kind: KongPlugin
metadata:
  name: jwt-auth
config:
  key_claim_name: iss
plugin: jwt
---
# Attach plugins to an Ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api
  annotations:
    konghq.com/plugins: rate-limit-api,jwt-auth
```

**OAuth2 Proxy — add OIDC authentication to any app:**

```yaml
# Deploy oauth2-proxy as a sidecar or separate deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: oauth2-proxy
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: oauth2-proxy
        image: quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:latest
        args:
        - --provider=github
        - --email-domain=company.com
        - --upstream=file:///dev/null
        - --http-address=0.0.0.0:4180
        env:
        - name: OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_ID
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: oauth2-proxy-secrets
              key: client-id
---
# Ingress uses oauth2-proxy for auth
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url: "http://oauth2-proxy.auth:4180/oauth2/auth"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-signin: "http://oauth2-proxy.auth:4180/oauth2/sign_in"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-response-headers: "X-Auth-Request-User,X-Auth-Request-Email"
```

**mTLS at the ingress layer:**

```yaml
# Require client certificates — mutual TLS
annotations:
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: default/ca-secret
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: "on"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-depth: "1"
  # Forward client cert info as headers to upstream
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-pass-certificate-to-upstream: "true"
```

sections.title: Exercise: deploy and configure nginx Ingress
sections.body:
## Exercise: End-to-End Ingress Configuration

This exercise builds a complete ingress setup from scratch: install the controller, deploy a test application, define routing rules, and verify rate limiting behavior. Each step maps to a real production workflow.

A few things to observe carefully as you work through this:

**Controller readiness before Ingress creation.** If you create an `Ingress` resource before the controller is running, Kubernetes will accept it (it's just a resource), but nothing will act on it. The controller must be running and watching the API before it can reconcile `Ingress` objects. The `kubectl wait` command in step 1 ensures this sequencing.

**How the controller translates your Ingress into nginx config.** Step 6 shows the actual `nginx.conf` that the controller generated from your `Ingress` resource. Reading it connects the high-level Kubernetes resource to the underlying reverse proxy configuration — and helps debug routing issues when requests aren't being forwarded as expected.

**Rate limiting behavior.** Step 5 uses a rapid loop to trigger the rate limiter. You will see `503` responses interspersed with `200` responses. The `503` is nginx's default response when a request is rejected by `limit_req`. In production, you would typically customize the error response code and body, and configure monitoring alerts on elevated `503` rates from the ingress layer.

**The `Host` header in test requests.** Step 4 sends requests with `-H 'Host: web-app.local'` because the ingress rule matches on the hostname, not the IP. Without this header, nginx would serve its default backend (typically a 404). In production, DNS resolves the hostname to the load balancer IP so clients automatically send the correct `Host` header; in this lab you simulate that with an explicit header.

Install the nginx Ingress Controller and expose a service with path-based routing and TLS.

```bash
# ── 1. Install nginx Ingress Controller ───────────────────────────────────
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm repo update

helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx --create-namespace \
  --set controller.service.type=NodePort \
  --set controller.service.nodePorts.http=30080 \
  --set controller.service.nodePorts.https=30443

# Wait for the controller to be ready
kubectl wait --namespace ingress-nginx \
  --for=condition=ready pod \
  --selector=app.kubernetes.io/component=controller \
  --timeout=120s

# ── 2. Deploy a test application ──────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -n learning -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: hashicorp/http-echo:latest
        args: ["-text=Hello from web-app"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5678
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  selector:
    app: web-app
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 5678
EOF

# ── 3. Create an Ingress ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -n learning -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-app
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: web-app.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-app
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

# ── 4. Test the Ingress ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Get the NodePort
NODE_PORT=$(kubectl get svc ingress-nginx-controller -n ingress-nginx \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[?(@.name=="http")].nodePort}')

# The k3s node is accessible as 'k3s' from within the Docker network
curl -H 'Host: web-app.local' http://k3s:${NODE_PORT}/
# Expected: Hello from web-app

# ── 5. Add rate limiting ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl annotate ingress web-app -n learning \
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps=5

# Test rate limiting with rapid requests
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
    -H 'Host: web-app.local' http://k3s:${NODE_PORT}/
done
# Some requests should return 503 (rate limited)

# ── 6. Inspect nginx config generated by the controller ──────────────────
kubectl exec -n ingress-nginx \
  $(kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx -l 'app.kubernetes.io/component=controller' -o name | head -1) \
  -- cat /etc/nginx/nginx.conf | grep -A5 'web-app.local'

# ── 7. Check Ingress status ───────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl describe ingress web-app -n learning

# ── 8. Clean up ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete deployment,service,ingress web-app -n learning
helm uninstall ingress-nginx -n ingress-nginx
```

questions.q: What is the main advantage of using a single Ingress Controller vs a LoadBalancer Service for each application?
options: Ingress controllers support UDP while LoadBalancer Services do not
One cloud load balancer shared across all apps — with path-based routing, TLS termination, and HTTP-layer features
Ingress controllers provide automatic horizontal scaling of your application
LoadBalancer Services require root access while Ingress does not
questions.explanation: Each cloud LoadBalancer Service provisions a separate cloud load balancer (typically $10-20/month each). An Ingress Controller uses one LoadBalancer to front all applications, routing by host/path. This reduces cost, centralizes TLS management, and allows HTTP-layer features like rate limiting and authentication.

questions.q: In Gateway API, which resource would an application team create to define routing rules for their service?
questions.explanation: Gateway API separates concerns: infrastructure teams manage GatewayClass (controller config), platform teams manage Gateway (ports, TLS, allowed namespaces), and application teams manage HTTPRoute (path routing, backend refs, traffic splitting). This role separation is a key improvement over Ingress where all config is in one resource.

questions.q: What does `pathType: Prefix` mean for an Ingress rule with `path: /api`?
options: Only requests with exactly the path `/api` are matched
Requests to `/api`, `/api/`, `/api/users`, and any sub-path are matched
The path is interpreted as a regular expression prefix
questions.explanation: With `pathType: Prefix`, the path `/api` matches any request whose URL path starts with `/api` — including `/api`, `/api/`, `/api/users/42`, etc. Use `pathType: Exact` to match only the specific path without any sub-paths.

sections.title: Challenge: multi-service Ingress with auth
sections.goal: Deploy two different services and expose them through a single Ingress Controller with path-based routing, TLS (self-signed), and basic authentication protecting one path while the other remains public.
hints: For basic auth: `htpasswd -c auth admin` then `kubectl create secret generic basic-auth --from-file=auth`
Apply TLS annotation `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: 'true'` and create a self-signed cert as a TLS Secret
Use two separate Ingress resources (one public, one with auth annotation) pointing to the same host — nginx merges them
success_criteria: Two services are deployed and accessible through the Ingress Controller
Path `/public` routes to one service with no authentication required
Path `/protected` routes to another service and returns 401 without credentials
TLS is configured — HTTPS works (self-signed cert is acceptable)
HTTP requests to port 80 redirect to HTTPS
